summary:
Ember is a web app that joins NASA's two fire-detection records, MODIS (from 2001) and VIIRS (from 2012), into one consistent burning calendar for India. VIIRS sees small fires that MODIS misses, so simply joining the records makes fire counts appear to jump 5.7 times in 2012. Ember learns that gap for each place and each month from the years both satellites flew (2012 to 2019), applies it to the MODIS-only years, and tests the result on 2020 to 2025, years it never saw. After correction the 2012 jump falls to 1.1 times, and India's corrected total sits within 3% of the real VIIRS count.
Anyone can search a town, district or state and see a typical year week by week, every year from 2001 to 2025, the usual reason fires happen at that time, and an accuracy readout for that area. Early-warning teams, emergency responders, scientists and land managers can see when burning usually starts, peaks and ends, and spot unusual years
details:
The problem. Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly. MODIS (Terra from 2000, Aqua from July 2002) sees mostly large fires at 1 km. VIIRS (from 2012) sees small fires too at 375 m. Joined as they are, India's counts jump 5.7 times in 2012. Fire managers are left without a consistent picture of when and where burning happens.

What Ember does. Ember harmonizes the two records into one burning-activity calendar for India, 2001 to 2025, covering 9.2 million corrected detections on a 27 km (0.25 degree) grid. A user searches any town, district or state and gets:

  • the busiest weeks of a typical year and the wider fire season;
  • a bar for every year from 2001 to 2025, marked "estimated from MODIS" (2001 to 2011) or "measured by VIIRS" (2012 on);
  • a map you can play year by year, with a before and after correction toggle;
  • the usual reason fires happen then, each with a cited news or research source;
  • an accuracy rating for that area, so users know how far to trust it.

How it works.

  1. Take the NASA FIRMS active fire records for India from both sensors and remove year-round heat sources such as coal fields (about 4% of the record, 308,099 detections).
  2. Count detections per grid cell per week, 52 weeks a year.
  3. In 2012 to 2019, when both satellites flew, learn how many VIIRS detections correspond to each MODIS detection, separately for each place and calendar month, leaning on the all-India ratio (about 5.6 times) where a place has few detections.
  4. Apply those ratios to the MODIS-only years, 2001 to 2011, so all 25 years sit on the VIIRS scale.
  5. Test on 2020 to 2025, six years the method never saw, comparing the corrected MODIS count with the real VIIRS count.

Results. The 2012 step falls from 5.7 times to 1.1 times (MODIS alone gives 1.0). On held-out years India's corrected weekly total is within 3% of VIIRS, against 82% too low with no correction.
